name: Natural TRT / "enclo + hCG" protocols

card.summary: Non-testosterone ways of raising testosterone, such as enclomiphene and hCG, that aim to avoid shutting down fertility; discussed as TRT alternatives, with limited evidence.
card.note: Enclomiphene is not approved in the US or EU; hCG and SERMs are prescription drugs.

quick.overview:
"Natural TRT" is a community label for approaches that raise the body's own testosterone production instead of replacing it with injected testosterone. The usual examples are enclomiphene, a selective estrogen receptor modulator, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a hormone that stimulates the testes.

The appeal described by proponents is keeping sperm production and testicular function. Medical sources describe hCG and clomiphene-type drugs as alternatives for some men with low testosterone, though evidence for enclomiphene is limited and it never received marketing approval.
quick.mechanism: Enclomiphene blocks estrogen's negative feedback at the pituitary, raising LH and FSH and so the testes' testosterone output. hCG acts on the LH receptor of the testes and stimulates testosterone production without suppressing sperm production, but it cannot work if the testes themselves cannot make testosterone [1][2].
quick.risks: Enclomiphene safety data in 1,403 participants listed headache, hot flush and nausea, with rare thromboembolic events and one fatal stroke. The EU's CHMP recommended refusing authorisation in 2018 and development was discontinued in 2021. Products sold online outside medical supervision are not regulated for quality [1].

lead: 'Natural TRT' (also 'enclo + hCG', non-suppressive TRT) is a community label for approaches that aim to raise a man's own testosterone by stimulating the pituitary-testicular axis rather than replacing testosterone with an injected or topical dose. The two drugs most often named are enclomiphene (enclomifene), a nonsteroidal selective estrogen receptor modulator, and human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), a gonadotropin that mimics luteinizing hormone (LH).[1][2][4] Clomiphene, the parent drug of enclomiphene, belongs to the same conversation.[10]

The appearance case, as proponents put it, runs through testosterone: higher levels are associated with muscle mass, leaner body composition, energy for training, libido and androgen-linked traits, and doing it through the body's own signalling is meant to keep testicular size, sperm production and fertility intact.[3][5] Exogenous testosterone can suppress spermatogenesis, which is why fertility-preserving options draw interest among men who want to conceive later.[3][2]

Clinical sources describe hCG and low-dose clomifene as alternatives to replacement for some men with hypogonadism, particularly when fertility matters.[2][10] Enclomiphene was developed for secondary hypogonadism but never obtained marketing approval: the European Medicines Agency's committee recommended refusing authorisation in 2018 and development stopped for all indications in 2021.[1] In bodybuilding the hCG half of the pairing is a long-standing component of post-cycle recovery routines, and on looksmax.org enclomiphene is discussed as a way of 'testosterone maxxing', including threads by teenage users, a pattern that sits alongside Wikipedia's note that hCG use in adolescents needs close monitoring for early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure.[4][7][11][12]

chain: Enclomiphene blocks estrogen feedback at the pituitary, raising LH and FSH; hCG mimics LH at the testes
Higher natural testosterone with fertility signalling kept active
More muscle, leaner body composition and training drive
angle.text: People use these protocols to raise testosterone, which influences muscle mass, body composition, libido and energy for training.[3][5] The distinguishing feature is that the body's own production is stimulated rather than replaced, with testicular function and fertility intended to stay active.[1][2]

paras: Enclomifene is the (E)-stereoisomer of clomifene, which is about 62 percent enclomifene and 38 percent zuclomifene; enclomifene is the more antiestrogenic of the two and zuclomifene the more estrogenic.[1][10] By blocking estrogen's negative feedback at the pituitary and hypothalamus it raises gonadotropin secretion and thereby testicular testosterone production.[1][10] Wikipedia describes enclomifene as studied mainly for men with secondary hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and, unlike testosterone replacement, not linked to reduced spermatogenesis.[1]

In secondary hypogonadism, where LH and FSH are normal or low, the testes can respond to gonadotropin stimulation; in primary hypogonadism LH is usually elevated and the testes themselves are impaired, so the approach is described as ineffective in true testicular failure.[2] Men's total testosterone is generally taken as normal at about 240 to 950 ng/dL depending on age, with treatment often considered for symptomatic values below about 230 ng/dL, and the Endocrine Society did not recommend screening men without symptoms as of 2018.[2]

Human chorionic gonadotropin binds the LH receptor on testicular Leydig cells and stimulates testosterone production, which in turn supports sperm production. It is used medically in some forms of hypogonadism, alone or alongside testosterone, and to treat or prevent infertility, including during testosterone replacement, where it helps preserve fertility and prevent testicular atrophy.[4][2]

Wikipedia lists cautions: prolonged treatment can increase androgen production, men with androgen-dependent tumours should not take it, and teenagers need close monitoring for early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure.[4] In bodybuilding, hCG is commonly used during and after anabolic steroid cycles to maintain testicular size and natural testosterone output.[4] It appears on some sports' banned lists, and athletes including baseball's Manny Ramirez (50-game ban, 2009) and the NFL's Brian Cushing have been sanctioned.[4]

A separate use of hCG, the 'hCG diet', paired low-dose hCG with a very-low-calorie diet from the 1950s; Wikipedia reports that a 1976 study and a 1995 meta-analysis found no advantage over dietary restriction, that the FDA and FTC moved against unapproved hCG weight-loss products in December 2011, and that the AMA in 2016 called its use for weight loss inappropriate.[4]

Clomifene was synthesised by Merrell chemists in 1956, patented in 1959 and approved in the United States in 1967 as Clomid for female infertility; use in men is off-label.[10] Wikipedia notes that at typical doses it roughly doubles to 2.5 times testosterone in hypogonadal men, that enclomifene clears in about 10 hours while zuclomifene lingers for days to weeks, and that a purified enclomifene product was reported to be about twice as effective at raising testosterone.[10] The hypogonadism article describes low-dose clomiphene as an alternative to replacement that avoids infertility and generally has few side effects at those doses.[2]

Wikipedia cites a 2013 comparison of oral enclomiphene with testosterone gel that reported maintained sperm counts alongside raised testosterone, and a 2014 study reporting that enclomiphene raised serum testosterone within 14 days in men with low testosterone.[1] Safety data from 1,403 participants in phase 2 and 3 studies listed headache (1.6 percent), hot flush (1.1 percent) and nausea (1.0 percent), with rarer events including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and one fatal ischemic stroke.[1] Wikipedia's clomifene article reports one large study in which 25 mg a day raised low testosterone from 309 to 642 ng/dL over three months, with total cholesterol falling and HDL, triglycerides, glucose and prolactin unchanged.[10] No published trial of an enclomiphene plus hCG combination was identified.

Enclomiphene was developed as Androxal and EnCyzix for male hypogonadism and type 2 diabetes. It was under FDA and EMA review by December 2016, the EMA's CHMP recommended refusing marketing authorisation in January 2018, and development was discontinued for all indications in April 2021.[1] Clomifene citrate is FDA-approved for ovulatory infertility and male use is off-label; WADA bans clomifene, and it can appear as an undeclared ingredient in black-market products.[10] hCG is a prescription drug; non-prescription hCG weight-loss products were targeted by US regulators in 2011.[4]

Wikipedia describes testosterone replacement as the classic treatment for male hypogonadism, with effects on libido and modest gains in physical activity and mood, and possible effects on spermatogenesis, hematocrit and sleep apnea.[3] A 2025 FDA decision, after the TRAVERSE trial found no increased cardiovascular risk versus placebo in hypogonadal men over a median 33 months, removed a boxed warning for cardiovascular risk; long-term safety remains unknown.[3] Suppressed spermatogenesis, which can cause infertility, is among its documented effects.[3]

The hypogonadism article notes that TRT generally suppresses sperm production and that men who want to conceive may be offered hCG or clomiphene, with testosterone often used for primary hypogonadism in men not seeking fertility.[2] An American College of Physicians guideline from 2020, summarised there, suggests discussing TRT for sexual dysfunction and says it may not be recommended for other reasons.[2]

On looksmax.org, enclomiphene is discussed as a testosterone-maximising compound; one thread title claims it gives users testosterone in the 90th to 99th percentile, and another is framed as a complete guide to 'testosterone maxxing' for users who consider themselves late developers.[7][8] Other threads cover use at age 15 to 17, sourcing questions, stacking with other compounds and questions about estrogen levels. These discussions often come from minors, and clinical labelling for hCG flags adolescents as needing close monitoring.[4] Some users report adverse experiences, for example fatigue and sleepiness after taking it.[6] In a thread asking whether enclomiphene could help with height or bones, a reply said it would do little unless testosterone is low and that growth hormone, not testosterone or DHT, is what matters for bone growth.[9]
A T Nation thread on testosterone and attracting the opposite sex shows the broader forum context in which testosterone is linked to social and physical outcomes.[5]

lore.intro: Enclomiphene and hCG are discussed on looksmax.org as ways to raise testosterone without injecting it, with side-effect reports, sourcing questions and use by teenagers appearing alongside enthusiasm.[6][7]

claims.claim: Enclomiphene can push testosterone into the 90th to 99th percentile
claims.believers: A thread title states this outright, and users present it as a strong non-suppressive way to raise testosterone.[7][8]
claims.experts: Trials cited by Wikipedia report raised serum testosterone in men with low testosterone and maintained sperm counts; the drug was not approved in the EU and development was discontinued.[1]

claims.claim: hCG keeps the testes active and fertile
claims.believers: Practitioners say hCG maintains testicular size and natural output during or after steroid use or replacement.[4]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes hCG as stimulating testosterone production without suppressing sperm production, and as used for fertility preservation during testosterone replacement.[2][4]

claims.claim: Enclomiphene may help bone growth or height
claims.believers: Some users ask whether it can aid height or bonemaxxing.[9]
claims.experts: Replies in the thread themselves note that growth hormone rather than testosterone or DHT drives bone growth, and no published trial tests enclomiphene for height; hCG labelling warns of premature growth-plate closure in adolescents.[9][4]

claims.believers: Some users describe taking it routinely as part of testosterone-focused routines.[8]
claims.experts: Clinical trial data list headache, hot flush and nausea, with rare thromboembolic events; one forum user reports feeling fatigued and sleepy after each use.[1][6]

claims.claim: Natural TRT avoids the drawbacks of testosterone replacement
claims.believers: Proponents emphasise preserved fertility and testicular size.[3][5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists fertility suppression as a documented effect of replacement and describes hCG and clomiphene as alternatives, while noting enclomiphene's non-approval and that hCG cannot work in testicular failure.[2][3][1]

claims.claim: Teenagers can use enclomiphene to boost development
claims.believers: Threads ask whether to start enclomiphene at 16 or 17 to support development.[11][12]
claims.experts: Clinical literature on enclomiphene studied adult men with hypogonadism; hCG labelling flags early sexual development and premature growth-plate closure in adolescents, and no located trial tests these compounds in healthy teenagers.[1][4]
